concerns.text: Ground truth derivation relies on a fixed drop threshold (≥0.1) and window (50 steps) without sensitivity analysis. If the true hacking signal magnitude varies by rubric type (e.g., 'Tone' vs 'Lexical'), a static threshold may systematically under-label one category, biasing the F1-score comparison and invalidating the generalization claim (SC-003).

The evaluation plan uses a paired t-test on F1-scores across seeds. However, F1-scores are bounded [0,1] and often non-normally distributed, especially with imbalanced classes (hacking is rare). A t-test may lack power or inflate Type I error. The plan does not justify normality or propose a non-parametric alternative (e.g., Wilcoxon) if assumptions fail, risking invalid significance claims (SC-002).

The z-score calculation uses a sliding window (W=20) to estimate local mean/std. If hacking events are prolonged (lasting >20 steps), the 'baseline' statistics will be contaminated by the anomaly itself, causing the z-score to be suppressed (regression to the mean) and reducing detection sensitivity. The plan lacks a mechanism to detect or exclude contaminated windows.

The detection logic flags timesteps if z(G(t)) > 3.0 OR ΔG(t) > k*σ. These two conditions are likely highly correlated (a spike in G(t) causes both high z and high ΔG). Using an OR condition without adjusting for multiple comparisons or dependency may inflate the false positive rate, making the 'static baseline' comparison unfair or the detector appear better than it is.

The plan assumes the CHERRL dataset contains 'J_unbiased' derived from an independent model. If 'J_unbiased' is actually a re-weighted version of 'J_biased' or shares training data with 'J_gold', the independence check (FR-006) might pass (low correlation) while the signals remain conceptually coupled, leading to circular validation that the statistical check cannot detect.
